extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent prosecution practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and documenting obviousness determinations during patent examination under 35 U.S.C. 103 (pre-AIA and AIA contexts), including Graham factual inquiries, rationales to support rejections, search scope, applicant reply and rebuttal evidence handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory nonobviousness standard (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the controlling statutory standard (pre-AIA language shown). Office rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 must be grounded in this standard and associated case law (e.g., KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible KSR approach to obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR reaffirmed the Graham framework but criticized overly rigid application of the TSM test; emphasized a flexible approach permitting use of common sense and ordinary creativity, while cautioning against hindsight bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should apply a flexible, functional approach consistent with KSR: consider predictable results, common sense inferences, and broader motivations to combine, but do not rely on conclusory statements; provide reasoned explanations. The decision lists four errors the Federal Circuit made (limiting to the patentee's problem, assuming POSA will look only to same-problem art, refusing 'obvious to try', and overemphasizing risk of hindsight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiry — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must read the specification and claims to understand the invention, give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification (Phillips v. AWH), then determine what to search for and where to search. See MPEP §§ 901-904, 2111, 2141.01(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiry — differences between claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims per MPEP §2111; consider both claimed limitations and the prior art collectively (see MPEP §2141.02). The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness (Dann v. Johnston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiry — level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings as to level of skill may be explicit or implicit (see MPEP §2141.03). Factors to consider include: type of problems encountered in the art; prior art solutions; rapidity of innovations; sophistication of technology; educational level of active workers (In re GPAC). A POSA is a person of ordinary creativity (KSR). Examiners may rely on their technical expertise in making this assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of objective evidence (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to obviousness ('secondary considerations') may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations should be evaluated case-by-case and included in the obviousness analysis when present. Evidence may be in the specification or submitted during prosecution; presentation does not automatically decide the issue — weight is determined on the facts (Graham). See MPEP §2145 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel as factfinders — requirement to record findings of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of the references applied; factual findings are the necessary underpinnings to establish obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making an obviousness rejection, include factual findings and provide explicit explanation of how those findings support the legal conclusion. 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notifying applicants of reasons for rejection. Failure to articulate findings may lead to appealable issues; rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements (In re Kahn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of POSA knowledge including common sense and general knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The focus is on what a person of ordinary skill in the pertinent art would have known and what such a person would have reasonably expected to do, regardless of whether knowledge came from documentary prior art, general knowledge in the art, or common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art is not limited to applied references; it includes the understanding of POSA. Examiners may rely on common sense and general knowledge where appropriate, but must support such reliance with reasoned explanation and, where necessary, evidence. Avoid hindsight by determining knowledge at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine claimed scope with broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply claim construction principles (Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111) before searching and before comparing to prior art. The determined scope drives what is searched and what prior art is pertinent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search scope — what to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and should also cover the disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching or suggestion to combine, a preferred search is directed to finding references that provide such teaching/suggestion if they exist. Follow MPEP §904 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search scope — where to search (analogous art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art can be either in the field of the inventor's endeavor or be reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the inventor was concerned; art from other fields may be considered if reasonably pertinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider analogous art principles (MPEP §2141.01(a), §1504.03). The KSR Court noted work in one field may prompt predictable variations in another; do not limit searches only to art solving the patentee's stated problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences — interpret claim language and consider whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting claim language (see MPEP §2111) and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document how specific claim limitations map (or do not map) to prior art disclosures. Consider whole-claim comparisons rather than isolated elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate level of ordinary skill in obviousness rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness rejection should include, either explicitly or implicitly in view of the prior art applied, an indication of the level of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding on level of skill may partially resolve obviousness. If implicit, show how prior art implies that level; when helpful, make an explicit finding. See MPEP §2141.03 for guidance on implicit indications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support obviousness rejections — combining known elements for predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results can support a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the combination would have been predictable to POSA and cite supporting references or common-knowledge rationale; reference KSR's guidance about predictable variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support obviousness rejections — simple substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that substituting one known element for another would produce expected results and that POSA would have had reason to make that substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support obviousness rejections — known technique used to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the technique was known and that POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of improvement when applied to the claimed device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support obviousness rejections — apply known technique to device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the device was 'ready for improvement' and that applying the technique would have been an obvious next step to POSA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support obviousness rejections — 'obvious to try' with finite predictable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success — can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when there are a limited number of predictable approaches and POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of success; differentiate from speculative or unpredictable experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support obviousness rejections — predictable cross-field variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations for use in the same or a different field when the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why cross-field adaptation would have been predictable (market forces, design incentives, known techniques). Cite supporting cases and technical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support obviousness rejections — teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While TSM should not be applied rigidly, it remains a valid rationale; identify any teaching/suggestion/motivation if present, or otherwise provide other rationales consistent with KSR. The list of rationales is illustrative, not exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonconclusory explanation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite factual findings and link them logically to the legal conclusion. Quoting In re Kahn and KSR: provide articulated reasoning rather than bare conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office's action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action; the reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office erred substantively as to the factual findings. Mere assertions that a prima facie case has not been made, without documentary support, are substantively inadequate and will not rebut the rejection under 37 CFR 1.111(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence timely presented by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination, including evidence of secondary considerations and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may show (A) technological difficulties preventing combination by known methods; (B) that elements in combination do not merely perform the same functions separately; or (C) the results were unexpected. After rebuttal, reconsider initial determination in view of entire record and articulate conclusions clearly (see MPEP §2145).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art availability — 35 U.S.C. 102 art usable under 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103. Admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a disclosure is not prior art under the appropriate section of 102 (e.g., overcome by timely declaration), it cannot be used in an obviousness rejection. See MPEP §§901-904, 2121-2129, 2151-2155 for prior art discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hindsight — determine prior art content at relevant time
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art is determined at the relevant time (time of invention for pre-AIA or before the effective filing date for AIA) to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers must cast their minds back to the relevant time and assess what POSA knew then. See MPEP §2145 subsection X.A. for dealing with applicant arguments that a rejection is based on hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) common ownership/joint research requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) to overcome a rejection based on prior art that qualifies only under certain subsections of pre-AIA 102, the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These disqualifications apply only to subject matter that qualifies as prior art solely under pre-AIA 102(e), (f), or (g) when used in a pre-AIA 103(a) rejection. See MPEP §§2146, 2146.01, 2146.02 for requirements and examples.
